javascript.label: JavaScript variable scope (var, let, const)
javascript.question: What is the difference between var, let and const in JavaScript?

keyPoints.point: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped
const cannot be reassigned (but an object it holds can still change)
var is hoisted and initialised as undefined; let/const are in the temporal dead zone

javascript.label: JavaScript closures
javascript.question: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give a small example of where you would use one.

keyPoints.point: A function remembers variables from the scope where it was created
It keeps access even after the outer function has returned
A practical use: private state, counters, callbacks or event handlers

javascript.label: JavaScript equality (== vs ===)
javascript.question: In JavaScript, what is the difference between == and ===? Which one would you use and why?

keyPoints.point: == converts types before comparing (type coercion)
=== compares value and type without conversion
Prefer === to avoid surprising results such as 0 == '' being true

javascript.label: The JavaScript event loop
javascript.question: JavaScript runs on a single thread. How does it still handle things like timers and network requests without freezing?

keyPoints.point: Slow work is handed to the browser/runtime (Web APIs) and runs in the background
Finished work puts a callback in a queue
The event loop runs queued callbacks when the call stack is empty

javascript.label: JavaScript promises and async/await
javascript.question: What is a Promise, and how does async/await relate to it?

keyPoints.point: A Promise represents a value that will be available later (pending, fulfilled, rejected)
Results are handled with then/catch
async/await is cleaner syntax over promises; await pauses the async function until it settles

dsa.label: Arrays vs linked lists
dsa.question: When would you choose a linked list over an array? Compare them for access and insertion.

keyPoints.point: Arrays give O(1) access by index; linked lists need O(n) to reach a position
Linked lists insert/delete in O(1) once you have the node; arrays shift elements, O(n)
Arrays are contiguous memory (cache friendly); linked lists store extra pointers

dsa.label: How hash maps work
dsa.question: How does a hash map give average O(1) lookups, and what can make it slower?

keyPoints.point: A hash function turns the key into a bucket index
Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing
Many collisions or a bad hash can degrade to O(n); resizing keeps the load factor low

dsa.label: Stacks vs queues
dsa.question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Give one real use of each.

keyPoints.point: A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO)
A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO)
Real uses: undo/call stack/bracket matching for stacks; BFS/task scheduling/printing for queues

dsa.label: Binary search
dsa.question: Explain binary search. What does it need from the input, and what is its time complexity?

keyPoints.point: The input must be sorted (or monotonic)
Compare with the middle and discard half each step
Runs in O(log n) time

dsa.label: BFS vs DFS
dsa.question: What is the difference between breadth-first search and depth-first search on a graph? When would you pick BFS?

keyPoints.point: BFS explores level by level using a queue
DFS goes deep first using a stack or recursion
BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph
